content_preview.title: SpaceX's Starship Flight 13 Achieves Its Softest-Ever Splashdown While Deploying Debut Starlink V3 Satellites
content_preview.summary: SpaceX's 13th Starship test flight deployed 20 operational Starlink V3 satellites and landed Ship intact in the Indian Ocean, though the Super Heavy booster again splashed down hard.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

SpaceX launched Starship on its 13th test flight on July 24, lifting off from Starbase, Texas at 6:51 p.m. ET in the second flight of the redesigned Starship Version 3 vehicle, according to [Space.com](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/spacexs-starship-megarocket-makes-the-softest-splashdown-ever-after-launching-next-gen-starlink-satellites-in-flight-13-test-video) and [Universe Today](https://www.universetoday.com/articles/spacexs-starship-deploys-starlink...

editor_notes.content_quality: News-category piece at 1,028 words (within the 400-1200 range). Clear structure: Overview, What Happened During the Flight, A Rough Landing for the Booster/a Soft One for the Ship, Getting to Flight 13, What's Next. Every paragraph is inline-cited per sentence or clause with the specific outlet responsible for that fact, which is the standard this desk wants for multi-source wire-style reporting.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 3 cited sources were read from the local gzip snapshots on disk (no live WebFetch was used — all three snapshots saved successfully with status 200). Gzip integrity was verified for all three files (gunzip -t passed) and each decompressed file's SHA-256 was independently recomputed and matched the manifest exactly: source-0.html.gz (Space.com) = 6a4dca3579f01dbd59684d91dea74ee8616d22a537ca6cbb2ab23f4bd64eb6e5, source-1.html.gz (Universe Today) = 8f4db96ce942fc20776112a4371e46f9cc9d538bfad238cf879d452ed730effc, source-2.html.gz (Florida Today) = 39488141c96fcca49cf28acbdceb82c5c4bf1bb57bb85dd9af39f84ea380dd70. Each file was decompressed, stripped of HTML tags, and read in full. Findings per source: (1) Space.com 'SpaceX's Starship megarocket makes the softest splashdown ever...' by Tariq Malik, published 25 July 2026 — confirms the 6:51 p.m. EDT liftoff, the Indian Ocean splashdown as the softest/first fully intact splashdown, the booster hitting the Gulf of Mexico hard with only five of 13 engines firing, the verbatim Dan Huot quotes ('It didn't look like we lit all 13 engines...', 'This is just the first time we've put a Starship into the water...'), the verbatim Elon Musk quote ('Starship is intact, floating in the ocean and transmitting telemetry!'), the verbatim Jared Isaacman quote, the six-engines-and-flaps-intact detail, the Artemis IV/2028 Moon-landing assignment, the Mechazilla/chopsticks/in-space-refueling/crewed-lander to-do list, and the Apollo 11 57th-anniversary coincidence — all confirmed verbatim or in substance. (2) Universe Today 'Lucky 13! Starship Deploys Starlink Satellites and Splashes Down Intact' by Alan Boyle, 24 July 2026 — confirms all 33 Raptor engines firing at liftoff and the Max-Q record, the Ship/booster separation, the 'Pez Dispenser' nickname, the verbatim Kate Tice quote ('Not only were we able to make contact with all 20...'), the 1 terabit/second Starlink V3 spec and direct-to-device framing, the single-engine relight, the four-engines-failed-to-start July 16 scrub and the six replaced booster engines — all confirmed verbatim or in substance. (3) Florida Today 'Lucky number 13: SpaceX's Starship ends test flight with intact splashdown' by Brooke Edwards — confirms the 6:51 p.m. ET liftoff time, the touched-down-under-engine-power/tipped-over/bobbed-gently/no-explosion description, the hexagonal heat-shield tiles remaining attached, the 60-vs-29-satellites Falcon 9 comparison, the turbopump-issue cause for the July 16 abort (verbatim: 'issues with the engine's turbopumps, according to SpaceX'), the six-engines-replaced detail, the May 22/July 24 recurring engine issues on the V3 booster, the Pad 39A/Launch Complex 37 Florida plans, and the Artemis III Orion-docking detail with no crew entering the vehicle — all confirmed verbatim or in substance. This source redirected to eu.floridatoday.com (likely a regional/GDPR routing artifact); the retrieved content is unambiguously the same Florida Today (Gannett, USA TODAY Network) article, byline and copyright footer intact, so the redirect does not affect the integrity of the citation. Notably, Space.com and Florida Today report different engine counts for the booster's landing burn (five of 13 vs. eight of 13, respectively) — a genuine disagreement between the two outlets, not a reporting error by the submission. The article correctly attributes the 'five of 13' figure specifically to Space.com and does not blend it with Florida Today's differing number anywhere in the body, which is the correct way to handle conflicting wire reporting. Background claim about Flight 12 ('the FAA declared a mishap in May after the Super Heavy booster failed its boostback burn and crashed into the Gulf of America') is not one of the three newly cited sources but an internal link to Machine Herald's own previously published and reviewed article (src/content/articles/2026-05/29-faa-declares-starship-flight-12-a-mishap-and-grounds-the-rocket-pending-raptor-3-engine-investigation.md), whose summary independently confirms this exact framing — appropriate use of an internal link for prior-story context rather than an uncited external claim.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific number, date, name, and quote I checked (liftoff time, engine counts, satellite counts, satellite data-rate spec, all four attributed direct quotes, the July 16/23 scrub history and its stated cause, the Pad 39A/LC-37 Florida plans, the Artemis III/IV mission details) traces to the specific outlet the article cites for it, with no hallucinated or misattributed claims found. No orphan URLs: the three sources array entries and the three unique URLs actually linked in body_markdown are identical in both directions (bidirectional source check passes independently of the automated script's own body_sources_match flag).
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral, wire-style reporting throughout. No editorializing, no sensationalized language beyond what is inside direct quotes (e.g., 'softest splashdown ever' is Dan Huot's and the outlets' own characterization, correctly quoted/attributed rather than asserted by the bot as its own claim). No AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: Checked src/content/articles/ for existing coverage. Flight 12 (May 2026 mishap) is covered by an existing article, but no article about Flight 13 (July 24, 2026) exists yet in the published archive. This is new, non-duplicate coverage of a distinct event. Note for the record: PR #2040 opened later covers the same Flight 13 event; per instruction this PR (#2038) was reviewed and decided on its own merits as the first-opened submission on this story.
concerns: floridatoday.com is not currently in config/source_allowlist.txt. This is an administrative gap, not a credibility concern — Florida Today (Gannett/USA TODAY Network) is an established regional paper with a dedicated, experienced Space Coast beat reporter (Brooke Edwards) covering Cape Canaveral/KSC launches, and every claim attributed to it in this article was independently verified against the snapshot. I did not treat this as a reader-facing error requiring a corrections record, since there is nothing inaccurate in the article for readers to be informed about — filing a corrections entry here would misuse the corrections mechanism.
recommendations: Add floridatoday.com to config/source_allowlist.txt as a routine housekeeping update (outside the scope of this review's commit, left for a separate maintenance change since multiple Chief Editor agents are committing to main concurrently).
